hacoo-links-not-working.title: Hacoo Links Not Working? Find the Missing Product
hacoo-links-not-working.description: A Hacoo link opens the app home, an unavailable item or the wrong option. Identify what happened, recover useful details and check a replacement before ordering.
sections: Start with the screen the link actually opens

Tap the saved link once and look at where you land. A feed full of unrelated posts means you reached the app without reaching the item. A product page carrying an unavailable message means the handoff got you further. A page selling a blue jacket when you saved a green one raises a different question about the selected option. Keep the first screen in view long enough to decide which case you have. The most useful detail to write down is the last thing that worked.

Save the original post or message before making changes. Include its date, the link as shared and the few words that describe the item. A screenshot of the destination alone loses the trail back to the person who shared it. If a friend sent several links in a row, match each URL with its own caption. One common and easily fixed mistake is opening the link beneath the next photograph. If you have already paid, skip the search altogether and open the transaction in the account you used to place the order.
When the app opens on its home screen

Start Hacoo from its normal app icon. Check whether you can open a post from the feed. If that works, go back to the original message and reopen the complete link. An address copied out of a long caption may have lost its final characters or picked up a full stop. Use the original share action when it is available. Avoid editing the address to guess what the missing part should have been. A small change can lead to an entirely different destination that still looks convincing.

If you first opened the link inside a social app, try opening that same address in your usual browser and use an app-opening control if the page offers one. Change just one thing on each attempt. You can then tell the person who shared it that the link opened a feed inside the social app but reached the correct post in your browser. Repeatedly reinstalling the app loses that information and can make it harder to find a post you were already able to view. If neither route reaches the product, move on to identifying it.
When the page says the item is unavailable

Keep the wording shown on the page. A sold-out colour, an unavailable size and a missing page each leave you with different options. Try another colour only as a check on whether the listing itself still works. Switch back before making any choice. A working black option tells you little about the stock of the brown option in the photograph. If the product page provides no explanation, keep the reason open. A single unavailable screen cannot establish a seller's motive or an issue with your account.

Hacoo describes its service as a community where independent people publish recommendations, and its terms allow content to be removed. A creator's old post may therefore remain useful for identifying a style even when it cannot take you to a current listing. Look for a later update by the original creator, or ask them to share the specific item again. A current link from that person is a stronger starting point than an undated repost of the same picture. Confirm the product again when it opens.
When the destination is live but the product looks different

Check the product name, the option currently highlighted and any caption beneath the gallery. Some galleries present several colours together. The picture that drew your eye may depict a different option from the one selected for purchase. Look for a second identifying feature that would survive a colour change. A jacket's pocket opening, the panel behind a trainer's heel or the point where a bag strap attaches can distinguish two otherwise similar designs. If the product description contradicts the photograph, record both details before deciding whether to continue.

Imagine a saved photo of a cream shoulder bag with a zip and a short handle. The replacement page opens on a beige bag with a magnetic closure, while a second gallery image shows a zip. Select the cream option and inspect its description and images again. If you still cannot connect the zip photograph to that option, ask which closure ships. If a zip is essential, an unanswered question is enough reason to keep looking. A matching product name adds very little if the feature you need belongs to another variant.
Recover an item from a screenshot or an old caption

Build a search phrase using details evident in the picture. For shoes, start with the silhouette, the fastening and the colour. For clothing, use the garment type and a distinctive construction detail. For a bag, the strap layout and fastening are often more helpful than a broad style label. Try a phrase such as “cream shoulder bag top zip short handle” before adding a brand you only think you recognise. Save the original spelling if the post includes a model number. Treat a code as a clue until you know which catalogue issued it.

Compare two or three possible matches side by side. Keep the original image in its own window so that your memory of it does not gradually change as you browse. A picture reused by several sellers gives you one visual reference repeated several times. Look for an independent distinguishing detail in the measurements, a second angle or the listed option. If the original photo never showed the back of the item, leave that comparison open. You can still recommend a similar style to a friend while describing exactly what remains unconfirmed.
Follow the route that belongs to your purchase

This guide's category directories take you to independent listings. A product number from one of those listings belongs to its destination catalogue. Searching for the same number inside Hacoo may bring up no result at all. Look at the final site's name before looking for the product again. If your aim is to place an order in Hacoo, its own ordering guide describes selecting the item inside the app and proceeding through the cart. For a purchase on a separate site, use the item details and order records provided there.

An old shopping link can disappear after payment while the order itself still exists. Find the receipt, identify the company that accepted payment, and use the matching order history. Note the order number, colour, size and date on that record. For a delivery question, open the tracking information associated with that order. Searching a current catalogue for another copy of the listing will tell you nothing reliable about the parcel already on its way. If support asks for the original product, send the old URL and the order reference together through its official channel.
Give the next person enough information to help

Send a short description of what you can reproduce. For example, explain that the link shared on Tuesday opens the Hacoo feed in your browser and in the app, that another shared post opens normally, and that the item you want is the cream, zipped version. Attach a cropped screenshot of the unexpected destination if useful. The person who shared the link can now check the right post and option. For an app problem, Hacoo's contact page points to in-app support. Keep personal order details in that private channel.

When a replacement link arrives, test the entire route once while you still have the original details to hand. Check the main picture, colour, size and distinguishing feature at the destination. If you intend to buy, check the same details in the cart and read the current total. Save the replacement under a descriptive name with the date you checked it. If the search only produced a similar item, label it as an alternative. That small distinction saves you from opening the same uncertain link a second time expecting an exact match.

hacoo-refund-status.title: Hacoo Refund Status: From Your Request to the Payment
hacoo-refund-status.description: Find the right Hacoo order, document a wrong or damaged item, follow return instructions and tell a refund approval apart from money reaching your account.
sections: Find the order and the last action recorded

Open the original order before contacting anyone about a Hacoo refund. Find the item, selected option and amount actually charged. Then open any after-sales conversation attached to that order. Write down the most recent action and its date. “I sent photos on Monday and received a request for the packaging label” tells you what to do next. “My refund has been pending since Monday” could describe several quite different stages and can lead both you and a support agent to investigate the wrong one.

Check who took the payment. A product guide, creator post or spreadsheet may have sent you to another merchant. The name on the order confirmation is a better starting point than the post where you discovered the item. If you bought through a separate service, open that service's order record and return instructions. If the purchase was made in Hacoo, enter the app through your normal route. Keep the order reference nearby and use the support options associated with the purchase. Public comments are a poor place to share a receipt or a shipping label.
Describe the issue in terms of one item

Separate what you ordered from what arrived. For a wrong colour, record the colour name on your order and the label on the product bag. For the wrong size, photograph the garment's or shoe's own label as well. A picture showing the item next to its associated packaging helps when several orders arrived together. Capture a whole-item view before taking a close-up of the problem. Someone unfamiliar with the product should be able to tell which part of the item the close-up shows.

The official Help Center asks for different evidence for damage, an incorrect product and a missing item. Use that distinction to keep your account useful. For damage, keep the outer and inner packaging until you receive instructions and photograph the affected area in good light. For a missing accessory, show what came in the package and identify the part shown in the order description. If an order contains several parcels, check the parcel breakdown first. One box without a second item does not establish that the second item was meant to be in that box.

Keep originals of the photographs and send the copies requested in the order conversation. Leave labels readable where support needs them. Crop unrelated household details and avoid posting the photographs publicly. A short note listing the item, the problem seen on arrival and the requested outcome is easier to follow than a long account of every attempt to get help. If a problem only appears during use, describe when it occurs and what you observed. Avoid giving a technical diagnosis when a clear description will do.
Read the instructions for this return

Hacoo's public policy pages describe more than one route. Its shipping page discusses after-sales help and situations where the customer keeps the item. Its dedicated returns policy also describes cases in which the company asks for the goods back. That same policy distinguishes a change of mind from a damaged or incorrect item, with packaging, condition and cost provisions depending on the case. Use those pages to understand which questions to ask, then read the instructions issued on your particular order.

Record any deadline in the order view when you begin. The public returns policy refers to a 15-day period after receipt for certain requests, subject to the item and conditions it describes. If you are still gathering photographs, contact the official order channel promptly instead of assuming an open message extends that window. Keep the item, packaging, accessories and tags together until you know which pieces the instructions cover. For a multiple-item order, label the correct bag now. Two similar barcodes are easy to mix up later.

Wait for the case-specific address or label before sending anything. The sender shown on the original parcel may be different from the location authorised to receive a return. If the instructions are unclear about postage, ask who arranges it and whether any expense is covered before paying a carrier. Where you are told to keep the item, save that message with the case. These details matter more to the next step than a general claim elsewhere that returns are always free or always require shipping.
Follow the request one decision at a time

A submission records that you asked for help. A message asking for another photograph is a request for evidence. An approval may authorise a return shipment or confirm an amount. Look at the verb and the object of the message together. “Return approved” can mean you may now send the item. “Refund issued to the original payment method” describes a later action. App wording can change, so follow what your screen says rather than trying to match it to a fixed list of status colours.

Imagine that two shirts arrived, one correct and one in the wrong size. Your message names only the second shirt. Support replies with a return label for that line item. Match the label to the shirt recorded in the case and check whether any accessories must accompany it. Keep a picture of the contents and the carrier receipt if the instructions require you to ship. A carrier delivery scan shows movement of a parcel. Reopen the case to see whether the contents have been checked and the refund itself has been issued.
Match the approved amount to the transaction

Read the amount and currency in the decision. Compare them with the amount allocated to the affected item, taking account of any discount or other adjustment shown on the original receipt. A price on today's product page cannot tell you exactly what you paid for that item in a previous basket. If only part of a set is missing, look for the amount actually approved. When it differs from what you expected, ask for the calculation and name the relevant line on the receipt.

Check the named destination of the money. A message about an account balance, a credit card refund and a payment-provider refund each points you to a different place. Hacoo's public guidance includes both a balance workflow and separate payment-method timings. Follow the destination on your own decision. An available promotional credit or review reward can appear in an account without being the refund in question. Match the amount, transaction description and date before treating any balance change as confirmation that the case is complete.
Read the date that starts the waiting period

For a request still under review, record the date it was submitted and the date of your last reply. For a required return, record the dispatch and delivery dates. Once a refund is issued, record that issue date and the method named. Counting from the day the original parcel arrived can make a payment appear overdue even when the refund decision happened much later. The public refund policy itself distinguishes time spent reviewing a request from time needed for the credit to appear.

Use the time range in the message attached to your transaction, including whether it counts working days. If the message gives no range, ask the official support team which date and method it is using. Check the transaction history for the named destination before asking for an update. If you see the correct amount there, record it. If the platform says it issued the refund but the payment provider cannot find it, request the refund reference, issue date and amount so the provider can trace the same transaction.
Ask for the one detail that is still missing

A useful follow-up can fit into a few sentences. For instance, state that the order contained two shirts, that the return of the blue shirt was delivered on the date shown by the carrier, and that the case still shows no refund decision. Ask whether the parcel has been matched to your case and whether anything else is needed. At the payment stage, replace the parcel details with the amount, date and payment destination. Keep the reply in the existing conversation so it remains attached to the evidence.

Close your record when the actual outcome matches the decision. That might mean money received at the stated destination, an alternative you accepted or a written explanation of an unresolved difference. Keep the final message beside the original receipt so you can reconcile a partial amount later. For a future order from the same creator or shop, keep its new evidence separate. A return instruction, address or refund route issued for the first purchase gives you no reliable instructions for the second.

hacoo-discount-code-not-working.title: Hacoo Discount Code Not Working? Check Your Cart Total
hacoo-discount-code-not-working.description: Check a missing promo field, a rejected Hacoo discount code or an unchanged checkout total. Work out the eligible amount before deciding whether to buy.
sections: Identify what failed before trying another code

Open the basket you intend to pay for and write down the displayed total in its own currency. Then note what actually happened. You might have reached a page with no coupon field, entered a code and received a message, or seen an offer accepted without the saving you expected. Each calls for a different check. A shopper who cannot find an input box gains little by collecting more codes. A shopper who already sees a discount line needs to read the amount rather than enter it again.

Check the destination at the top of the page or in the order flow. An independent Hacoo product directory may lead to a separate shop. A code advertised for a purchase inside the Hacoo app belongs to the offer described by that promotion. Something displayed on a guide cannot make another seller accept it. Hacoo's official ordering help describes choosing an item in the app, adding it to the cart and checking out there. Start with that route if the offer specifically says it applies to an in-app order.
Look for the offer on the route where you can use it

Read the account and checkout screens for the descriptions they actually show. A voucher saved to your account may be offered for selection, while a manually entered code would need an input field. A reduction attached to a particular product may already be reflected in its price. Open any visible price breakdown before deciding a code is missing. The presence of a wallet does not tell you that every order accepts a typed promo code. Hacoo's public order guide does not specify that every customer sees the same coupon field.

Go back to the original offer and check its instructions. A typed sequence appearing at the end of a creator's caption is a lead, not confirmation that the offer is available on your account today. Look for the exact destination, the redemption action and any dates attached to it. If the source directs you to claim an offer first, check whether your account actually displays that step. Avoid following a link that asks for a payment, login code or card details simply to reveal a coupon. Use the official checkout to review your basket.
Read the condition that applies to your basket

Start with the words accompanying the offer. Check whether it names a particular country, account type, basket amount, product selection or period of use. These are questions to ask of that offer, rather than assumptions about all Hacoo promotions. If it says “first order,” do not treat an existing customer's screenshot as evidence that your own account qualifies. Likewise, a page showing an offer in another currency may describe a different campaign. A brief note of the actual terms is more useful than a collection of recent-looking codes without conditions.

When terms mention a minimum purchase, look for what counts towards it. The full payable total can include delivery or items outside the promotion. Minimums, where specified, may refer to an eligible subtotal. If the offer has a ceiling on the saving, make a note of the ceiling as well as the advertised percentage. If no rule is published, keep the answer open and inspect the price breakdown. Changing your delivery address to an address you cannot receive parcels at will give you a misleading result even if a different offer appears.
Reproduce a rejection with a single change

Copy the code from its source, preserving any characters and spelling shown there. Check for a trailing full stop or space copied from the surrounding text. Read the response before altering the rest of the basket. An expired-offer message gives you something specific to verify against the promotion dates. A message about the order amount calls for checking the qualifying items. A general rejection gives less information. Record its exact wording rather than guessing it means the account has been restricted.

Keep quantity, currency, destination and selected options unchanged during the next check. If the promotion names particular items, compare a qualifying item and the one you planned to buy with the rest of the conditions held steady. You can inspect a basket without placing the order. When one item works and the other does not, check the eligibility wording again. If the promotion names no qualifying products and neither line shows a saving, stop testing unrelated items. Ask about the specific offer and item, or make your decision on the price you can see.
Work out the reduction using the eligible amount

Consider a fictional basket in euros. A hoodie costs €48, a cap costs €12 and delivery is €5. Suppose the offer says ten percent off the hoodie only. The eligible amount is €48 and the saving is €4.80. The payable total would fall from €65 to €60.20, assuming every other line stays the same. Ten percent of €65 would be €6.50, but that calculation includes the cap and delivery. This example illustrates the arithmetic. The prices and percentage are not a current Hacoo promotion.

Now suppose the same fictional offer requires €50 of eligible merchandise. The hoodie alone comes to €48. An ineligible €12 cap takes the merchandise total to €60 yet contributes nothing to that threshold. Buying something extra just to cross a threshold can also cost more overall. If an eligible €8 item brings eligible spending to €56, a ten percent reduction saves €5.60. With the cap and delivery unchanged you would pay €67.40, which is more than the original €65 basket. Compare what you will pay for the items you want before adding anything.
Read the final order summary after every change

Take the amount you noted at the start and compare the final lines in the same currency. Look at each item price, quantity, any savings already applied, delivery and the final payable amount. If the offer replaces an earlier saving, the extra reduction can be smaller than the headline rate. For example, replacing a €4 discount with a €5 discount reduces the previous total by €1. Only use that explanation if the before-and-after lines show the original discount being removed. A similar-looking total by itself does not establish what changed.

A reward tied to a future action deserves its own check. Hacoo's review cashback help describes a reward associated with reviewing an eligible delivered item, and directs users to their wallet to check it. That is different from an immediate reduction on the purchase in front of you. Check which figure describes today's payment and which describes a possible later benefit. If a creator speaks about “getting money back,” inspect the actual offer wording. Treating a later wallet reward as an immediate saving leaves an unexplained difference on the payment screen.
Decide before paying and save a useful record

If the final total works for you, review it once more after selecting the shipping option and before confirming payment. If the reduction is essential and the total remains too high, leave the order unpaid while you check the offer. Completing a transaction solely to see whether a discount appears afterwards is a poor way to verify eligibility. The order review in front of you is a much stronger basis for a decision than a promise in a comment or a price from an old screenshot.

For an unresolved case, contact the support route for the site where you are checking out. Describe the offer source, country, currency, eligible product, subtotal and exact response. A cropped screenshot of the price breakdown is usually more informative than a photograph of an entire phone screen. Hide full payment and personal details. Ask which condition applies to the item or where a claimed voucher should appear for that order. If you already paid, include the order reference privately and ask what amount was recorded. Keep the confirmation and the reply together.

hacoo-shoes-finds.title: Hacoo Shoes Finds: Sneaker Links, Photos and Size Checks
hacoo-shoes-finds.description: Browse footwear finds, measure both feet, read a listing's centimetre chart and compare the exact sneaker colour and size before opening the final checkout.
sections: Start with a pair you would actually wear

Open the footwear category when you want to compare several pairs. A product link takes you to one listing and is most useful after you have narrowed your choice. Before browsing, write down two requirements that would make you reject a shoe. You might need a wide forefoot and a low collar, or a particular fastening you can adjust while standing. With those requirements in mind, a missing width description or a decorative strap becomes a specific question to answer rather than a surprise after delivery.

Make a small shortlist from the results. Three low-top trainers with similar purposes are easier to compare than a board full of unrelated silhouettes. Save the destination, the colour and the size system shown for each. Write down what you liked in the original photo as well. A low cream trainer with a dark heel panel is more useful as a description than “the pair from yesterday.” A creator's caption, an independent listing and the official app can use different titles for similar-looking shoes. Keep the source attached to each item.
Measure both feet and keep the unit

Take the measurement on a firm floor with the socks you expect to wear. Use a sheet of paper that fits the whole foot and mark the back of the heel and the end of the longest toe while standing normally. The longest toe is not necessarily the big toe. Measure the straight distance between those marks with a ruler and record it in millimetres or centimetres. Repeat on the other foot. If a mark looks slanted or the paper moved, repeat that measurement instead of rounding to a familiar size.

Suppose the two measurements are 25.4 cm and 25.8 cm. Keep both values, with 25.8 cm as the longer foot to compare against the listing's guidance. If the chart specifies an alternative measuring method, follow that method before comparing the value. A figure measured standing on paper is a foot length. A stamp reading “26” on another shoe might represent a manufacturer's size designation. An insole removed from that shoe is a component with its own dimensions. Treating all three as interchangeable can point to a different row of the chart.

A comfortable pair you own adds context. Note whether your heel sits securely, whether the forefoot feels snug and which socks you normally use with that pair. Measurements taken from a removable insole can help only when the seller supplies the equivalent measurement and both methods agree. A curved heel cup or a raised front edge can change where the ruler starts and ends. If the listing gives no definition, ask what was actually measured before comparing the numbers.
Read the chart for the model and selected size

Look at the column headings and the units before finding your usual size. A chart labelled “recommended foot length” is offering guidance about the foot that fits. A chart labelled “insole length” is describing the shoe, leaving a different question about usable space. Some pages show EU, UK and US labels together. Check the series and the model attached to those labels. A conversion table copied from another maker will not resolve an unexplained centimetre value on the listing you intend to order.

For the shopper with a 25.8 cm longer foot, imagine one listing gives a recommended range of 25.6–26.0 cm for a particular option. That option merits a closer look. A second listing says only “26.0 cm” beside the same size label. Ask whether it means recommended foot length, insole length or a label value. The figures look similar but only the first listing answered the actual question. Avoid adding a fixed allowance just because another reviewer suggests it. The chart may already include the maker's intended allowance.
Compare shape after checking length

A shoe can accommodate the measured length and still press at the sides. Compare the front shape with a pair you know. Look for a picture from above that shows how quickly the toe tapers and where the widest part appears. A side view can help you see a low collar or a high padded tongue. These details help you decide what to ask. They cannot tell you the exact internal width from a photograph, especially when the shoes in the two images are different sizes.

If width matters, ask which width options or dimensions apply to your selected size. If your existing issue is heel slip, look at the collar and fastening and ask whether they allow the adjustment you need. Choosing a longer size changes more than width and may move the shoe's flex point or leave excess room at the heel. The aim is to resolve the particular fit issue you have. A comment that a shoe “runs small” leaves open whether the reviewer experienced short length, narrow width or a low toe box.
Use the photos to check the exact option

Start with both sides, then look at the rear, toe and outsole. Note a distinguishing detail, such as a heel overlay, a panel seam or the tread shape. Change to the colour you actually want and see whether the gallery changes with it. A cream pair with an off-white sole and a white pair with a contrasting sole may share the same first picture. The colour selected in the cart matters more than the photo that originally attracted you. If the site uses codes for colours, save the code beside its written description.

Compare each claim with the view that could support it. An outsole picture can show a tread pattern. It cannot demonstrate grip on a wet surface. A label close-up can help identify a size series but cannot establish that the pair will fit your foot or verify its origin. A buyer's picture describes the pair that person received, provided the variant is clear. A catalogue picture describes the listing's presentation. If you need a view of an inside seam, request that view. More photographs of the outside will leave the same uncertainty.
Choose between comparable listings

Use a line of notes per exact option with the product title, selected colour, size, chart definition, price in the displayed currency and date checked. Finish each line with one question that could change your decision. For example, pair A provides a defined foot-length range and a clear rear view. Pair B has a more suitable shape but provides no size definition. Ask the seller of pair B which measurement is shown. If the answer arrives, update that line rather than guessing a score for both pairs.

Read reviews selectively. A person who gives their longer foot length, selected size, width preference and the same model offers a comparison you can test. A brief “take your usual size” omits those reference points. Reviews of a different colour may still explain lace adjustment or the location of a seam, but check that the construction actually matches. Keep an eye on the age of the review and whether the listing has changed since. Even a first-hand review of a confirmed pair cannot establish what every later batch will be like.
Check the basket and save the pair you chose

Open the chosen listing again from your shortlist before buying. Select the colour, then size, and check whether either selection changes stock, price or delivery information. Compare the option in the basket with your notes. If the gallery shows an attractive alternative after your size sells out, evaluate it separately. For a pair intended for a particular event, read the delivery estimate at the destination with the actual address and shipping service selected. Keep delivery timing and fit as two separate decisions.

Look at the merchant on the payment screen and read its current size-related return conditions. An independent product directory and a purchase inside Hacoo may lead to different merchants and support routes. Save the order confirmation, selected variant and relevant chart together. That gives you the starting point for checking the parcel when it arrives. If the only unresolved point is essential, such as whether the chart describes foot length, keep the pair on your shortlist and wait for a precise answer.

hacoo-clothing-finds.title: Hacoo Clothing Finds: Hoodie, T-Shirt and Jacket Size Checks
hacoo-clothing-finds.description: Choose a clothing category, compare flat garment measurements and see how to check a hoodie, T-shirt or jacket for the cut and layers you want.
sections: Choose a category and a reference garment

Start in the hoodie, T-shirt or jacket category if you want to compare several garments. A single product link is a shortcut to one item and may reopen with a different colour selected. Decide what job the garment has to do before saving it. A hoodie you want to layer under a coat needs a different shoulder and sleeve shape from one you plan to wear over a thick sweatshirt. A T-shirt for tucking in puts more emphasis on body length than one you want to wear loose.

Choose something from your wardrobe that already works for that purpose. It is worth getting the actual garment out instead of relying on a size you remember buying. Look at where it sits at the hem, how the sleeves end and whether you want the new item to be wider or shorter. Record the material and whether it has stretched or shrunk with wear. A favourite washed cotton tee still gives you a useful target for the fit you enjoy, even if its dimensions have changed since you bought it.
Put the seller's numbers and yours on the same basis

Lay your reference garment on a flat surface and smooth obvious folds without stretching the fabric. For chest width, measure straight across between the underarm points. For body length, choose a starting point and record it, such as the high shoulder beside the collar down to the hem. Measure the shoulder seam to seam if the garment has visible shoulder seams. For a sleeve, note whether you began at the shoulder seam, collar or centre back. A useful note contains the endpoints as well as the number.

Now look for the diagram or instructions on the listing. A measurement of 56 cm across a sweatshirt lying flat is not a body chest measurement. Doubling it gives an approximate garment circumference at that point. It still describes the garment and includes the space its cut provides. Do not compare that doubled figure directly with a suggested body-chest range unless the listing explains the relationship. If the chart gives inches and you measured centimetres, convert once, record both units and keep the original number for checking.

Imagine your reference hoodie measures 56 cm across the chest and 66 cm from the high shoulder to the hem. A candidate measured by the same method is 59 cm across and 62 cm long. It would give you about 6 cm more circumference at chest level and 4 cm less length. That might be exactly right over high-waisted trousers and a poor match if you wanted more coverage. Calling the new hoodie “larger” misses the decision. It is wider and shorter by different amounts.
For a hoodie, check the hem and the shoulders

A thick-looking hood and a large chest measurement can make a hoodie look roomy in a photograph. Check where the shoulder seam sits and how the sleeve measurement was taken. A dropped seam moves the starting point down the arm, so a shorter shoulder-to-cuff measurement can still give a long overall reach. If you own a hoodie with a similar shoulder, take a collar-to-cuff measurement from both when the listing permits it. If the methods differ, write down the uncertainty before choosing a size.

Look closely at the hem. A close ribbed band can make a wide hoodie sit at the waist, while a looser hem can fall over the hips. For a zip style, inspect the fastening and pocket position on the selected colour. If you expect to wear it open, consider how the panels hang in the available photographs. For a pullover, check the hood opening and neckline. When warmth or weight matters, look for a stated composition or fabric weight. Studio lighting and the thickness of a folded pile tell you little about how the garment feels in use.
For a T-shirt, look past the graphic

Compare chest width, body length and sleeve opening as a set. Two T-shirts with an identical width can fit very differently if one has a long narrow sleeve and the other ends loosely above the elbow. Check a front and rear view for the placement of side seams, graphic and neckline. A graphic shown separately on a plain background may tell you the intended design without showing the size or position of the print on the garment you would receive.

Look for photographs taken in the selected colour. An image of a dark option gives limited information about the opacity of a white one. If fabric composition or care matters, find the stated description or a readable label for that item. An image of a bright print cannot establish wash durability. A buyer photograph taken after several washes can contribute one person's experience if it identifies the same variant and explains how it was washed. Save that detail separately from the seller's care instructions. If the image supplies neither size nor context, use it for visual reference only.
For a jacket, test the layer you intend to wear

Put on your existing jacket over the kind of garment you plan to wear underneath. Close it, reach forwards and bend your arms. Notice where movement is restricted. A snug upper arm, short sleeve or tight shoulder each points to a different measurement to investigate. Measure the reference jacket while it lies flat, using the selected listing's method where possible. Outer chest width alone cannot establish the usable room inside a lined or padded jacket. If you need room for a sweatshirt, ask about the relevant dimension on the finished garment.

Inspect the closure, pockets and lining on the actual colour option. A flap in the front view can cover a working pocket, a shallow opening or decoration. If you need a secure pocket for a particular object, ask for the usable opening and depth. A detachable hood should have a fastening or description that supports the claim. A jacket photographed in snow may be styled for winter while offering no tested temperature or waterproof rating. Base the choice on the details the listing actually gives and on how you expect to use the jacket.
Make a shortlist you can return to

Keep each candidate's final URL, selected size and colour, measurement method, price and one deciding question. For two black jackets with similar fronts, label one by its stitched cuffs and the other by its button cuffs. These details help when a gallery resets or an old link opens a general feed. If the listing points to a different shopper, seller or checkout site after a redirect, confirm the actual garment before transferring information from your earlier notes.

When two items look equally suitable, compare what remains unknown. A hoodie with a clearly defined width and length may still leave its sleeve method unresolved. A second hoodie may offer better sleeve measurements but have an unconfirmed hem width. If you care most about the sleeve covering your wrist when cycling, the first seller's missing measurement takes priority. Ask a specific question with endpoints and units. A request for the measurement from the base of the collar to the cuff on size M gives a clearer answer than asking whether the seller thinks it runs large.
Check the selected garment through to checkout

Reopen the chosen product and check whether changing colour alters the size menu, material wording, price or gallery. Read the current total with the destination and delivery option you would use. A product found through a Hacoo clothing spreadsheet can open an independent catalogue. Read the order and returns information belonging to the merchant that will take the payment. If you are ordering inside the Hacoo app, use that order's checkout details and keep its confirmation for later support.

Finally, compare the basket description against your shortlist one line at a time. Make sure the garment type, option, quantity and size refer to the item you measured for. Save the relevant size chart with the purchase details while it is still available. If a jacket arrives with a different label, you will have the exact order to compare it with. If the softer blue T-shirt was merely a picture from another colourway, you can catch the mismatch now. A few minutes spent on the selected variant matter more than adding another promising photograph to your list.
